claim: ATP-sensitive K+ (KATP) channels in pancreatic β cells are comprised of pore-forming subunits (Kir6.2) and modulatory sulfonylurea receptor subunits (SUR1).
source: ATP-sensitive K+ (KATP) channels in pancreatic β cells are comprised of pore-forming subunits (Kir6.2) and modulatory sulfonylurea receptor subunits (SUR1).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about the composition of KATP channels in pancreatic β cells.

claim: The ATP sensitivity of KATP channels enables them to couple metabolic state to insulin secretion in β cells.
source: The ATP sensitivity of these channels enables them to couple metabolic state to insulin secretion in β cells.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about the function of KATP channels.

claim: Glibenclamide targets SUR1 and indirectly suppresses Kir6.2 activity.
source: Antidiabetic sulfonylureas such as glibenclamide target SUR1 and indirectly suppress Kir6.2 activity.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the mechanism of action of glibenclamide.

claim: Glibenclamide acts as both a primary and a secondary secretagogue to trigger insulin secretion and potentiate glucose-stimulated insulin secretion.
source: Glibenclamide acts as both a primary and a secondary secretagogue to trigger insulin secretion and potentiate glucose-stimulated insulin secretion, respectively.
evidence: This is established knowledge about glibenclamide's effects on insulin secretion.

claim: SpTx1 acts as a strong secondary, but not a strong primary, secretagogue.
source: We tested whether blocking Kir6.2 itself causes the same effects as glibenclamide, and found that the Kir6.2 pore-blocking venom toxin SpTx1 acts as a strong secondary, but not a strong primary, secretagogue.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: SpTx1 triggered a transient rise of plasma insulin in diabetic mice overexpressing Kir6.2.
source: SpTx1 triggered a transient rise of plasma insulin and lowered the elevated blood glucose of diabetic mice overexpressing Kir6.2 but did not affect those of nondiabetic mice.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8.

claim: SpTx1 lowered the elevated blood glucose of diabetic mice overexpressing Kir6.2.
source: SpTx1 triggered a transient rise of plasma insulin and lowered the elevated blood glucose of diabetic mice overexpressing Kir6.2 but did not affect those of nondiabetic mice.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8.

claim: SpTx1 did not affect plasma insulin or blood glucose of nondiabetic mice.
source: SpTx1 triggered a transient rise of plasma insulin and lowered the elevated blood glucose of diabetic mice overexpressing Kir6.2 but did not affect those of nondiabetic mice.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1 and 8.

claim: Neonatal diabetes mellitus (NDM) was traditionally considered a variant in Type 1 diabetes mellitus (T1DM).
source: Among these diseases, neonatal diabetes mellitus (NDM) was traditionally considered a variant in Type 1 diabetes mellitus (T1DM) and had accordingly been treated with insulin.
evidence: This is historical medical knowledge about the classification of NDM.

claim: NDM has been recognized as a genetic disorder that stems from gain-of-function mutations in pancreatic ATP-sensitive K+ (KATP) channels since the early 2000s.
source: Since the early 2000s, NDM has been recognized as a genetic disorder that stems from gain-of-function mutations in pancreatic ATP-sensitive K+ (KATP) channels (Gloyn et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Gloyn et al., 2004.

claim: Each KATP channel protein complex consists of four pore-forming inward-rectifier 6.2 (Kcnj11 or Kir6.2) subunits and four surrounding auxiliary sulfonylurea receptor 1 (Abcc8 or SUR1) subunits.
source: The octameric KATP channel protein complexes, each of which consists of four pore-forming inward-rectifier 6.2 (Kcnj11 or Kir6.2) subunits and four surrounding auxiliary sulfonylurea receptor 1 (Abcc8 or SUR1) subunits (Aguilar-Bryan et al., 1995; Inagaki et al., 1995), are present in the plasma membrane of β cells within islets of Langerhans in the pancreas.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Aguilar-Bryan et al., 1995 and Inagaki et al., 1995.

claim: KATP channel protein complexes are present in the plasma membrane of β cells within islets of Langerhans in the pancreas.
source: The octameric KATP channel protein complexes, each of which consists of four pore-forming inward-rectifier 6.2 (Kcnj11 or Kir6.2) subunits and four surrounding auxiliary sulfonylurea receptor 1 (Abcc8 or SUR1) subunits (Aguilar-Bryan et al., 1995; Inagaki et al., 1995), are present in the plasma membrane of β cells within islets of Langerhans in the pancreas.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the location of KATP channels.

claim: Expression of Kir6.2 with gain-of-function mutations in mice caused hypoinsulinemia and hyperglycemia.
source: The discovery of the mutations underlying NDM was anticipated by the experimental demonstration in mice that the expression of Kir6.2 with gain-of-function mutations caused hypoinsulinemia and hyperglycemia (Koster et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Koster et al., 2000.

claim: Mutations in Kir6.2 tend to cause more severe phenotypes of NDM than those in SUR1.
source: Mutations in Kir6.2 tend to cause more severe phenotypes of NDM than those in SUR1, and the hyperactivity of the resulting mutant KATP channels is less likely to be adequately suppressed by sulfonylureas (Hattersley and Ashcroft, 2005; Pipatpolkai et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Hattersley and Ashcroft, 2005 and Pipatpolkai et al., 2020.

claim: The hyperactivity of mutant KATP channels from Kir6.2 mutations is less likely to be adequately suppressed by sulfonylureas.
source: Mutations in Kir6.2 tend to cause more severe phenotypes of NDM than those in SUR1, and the hyperactivity of the resulting mutant KATP channels is less likely to be adequately suppressed by sulfonylureas (Hattersley and Ashcroft, 2005; Pipatpolkai et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Hattersley and Ashcroft, 2005 and Pipatpolkai et al., 2020.

claim: Severe-phenotype-causing mutations of Kir6.2 are associated with developmental delay, epilepsy, and permanent neonatal diabetes (DEND syndrome).
source: The severe-phenotype-causing mutations of Kir6.2 are also associated with developmental delay, epilepsy, and permanent neonatal diabetes (DEND syndrome).
evidence: This is established medical knowledge about DEND syndrome.

claim: KATP channels were originally discovered in the plasma membrane of cardiac myocytes.
source: KATP channels were originally discovered in the plasma membrane of cardiac myocytes (Noma, 1983) and later found to exist in many other tissue types.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Noma, 1983.

claim: KATP channels in pancreatic β cells are inhibited by both extracellular glucose and intracellular ATP.
source: KATP channels in pancreatic β cells are inhibited by both extracellular glucose and intracellular ATP (Ashcroft et al., 1984; Rorsman and Trube, 1985).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Ashcroft et al., 1984 and Rorsman and Trube, 1985.

claim: When blood glucose concentration is low, the overall metabolism in β cells remains low and KATP channels tend to be open, helping to maintain the hyperpolarized resting membrane potential.
source: When the blood glucose concentration is low, the overall metabolism in β cells remains low. Consequently, the ratio of intracellular ATP to ADP is relatively low, and the KATP channels tend to be open, helping to maintain the hyperpolarized resting membrane potential (Vm).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the mechanism of KATP channel regulation of membrane potential.

claim: An elevated blood glucose level increases the metabolism in β cells and thus the ratio of intracellular ATP to ADP.
source: An elevated blood glucose level increases the metabolism in β cells and thus the ratio of intracellular ATP to ADP.
evidence: This is established knowledge about glucose metabolism in β cells.

claim: An increase in ATP relative to ADP inhibits KATP channels, depolarizing Vm and thereby increasing the voltage-gated Ca2+ channel (CaV) activity.
source: An increase in ATP relative to ADP inhibits KATP channels, depolarizing Vm and thereby increasing the voltage-gated Ca2+ channel (CaV) activity.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the excitation-secretion coupling mechanism in β cells.

claim: An increased CaV-mediated Ca2+ influx raises the concentration of intracellular free Ca2+ ([Ca2+]in), a signal required for triggering robust exocytotic secretion of insulin.
source: An increased CaV-mediated Ca2+ influx raises the concentration of intracellular free Ca2+ ([Ca2+]in), a signal required for triggering robust exocytotic secretion of insulin.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the role of calcium in insulin secretion.

claim: Sulfonylureas act as impactful primary secretagogues, triggering insulin release in the presence of a nonstimulating, basal concentration of glucose.
source: As a class of the antidiabetic drugs, sulfonylureas act as impactful primary secretagogues, triggering insulin release in the presence of a nonstimulating, basal concentration of glucose.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the pharmacological action of sulfonylureas.

claim: Sulfonylureas act as strong secondary secretagogues, robustly potentiating the insulin secretion stimulated by an elevated concentration of glucose.
source: These drugs also act as strong secondary secretagogues, robustly potentiating the insulin secretion stimulated by an elevated concentration of glucose.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the pharmacological action of sulfonylureas.

claim: Sulfonylureas bind to SUR1 and thereby indirectly inhibit currents through the KATP channels.
source: Sulfonylureas bind to SUR1 and thereby indirectly inhibit currents through the KATP channels (Gribble and Reimann, 2003; Henquin, 1992).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Gribble and Reimann, 2003 and Henquin, 1992.

claim: Glibenclamide is membrane permeable and has been shown to lodge inside SUR1.
source: The commonly used sulfonylurea glibenclamide is membrane permeable and has been shown to lodge inside SUR1, and its effect on insulin secretion cannot be rapidly reversed (Lee et al., 2017; Li et al., 2017; Martin et al., 2017; Schatz et al., 1977; Wu et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Lee et al., 2017; Li et al., 2017; Martin et al., 2017; Schatz et al., 1977; Wu et al., 2018.

claim: The effect of glibenclamide on insulin secretion cannot be rapidly reversed.
source: The commonly used sulfonylurea glibenclamide is membrane permeable and has been shown to lodge inside SUR1, and its effect on insulin secretion cannot be rapidly reversed (Lee et al., 2017; Li et al., 2017; Martin et al., 2017; Schatz et al., 1977; Wu et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Lee et al., 2017; Li et al., 2017; Martin et al., 2017; Schatz et al., 1977; Wu et al., 2018.

claim: Some studies have suggested that glibenclamide also interacts with other proteins involved in the secretory process, in addition to KATP channels in the plasma membrane.
source: However, some studies have suggested that glibenclamide also interacts with other proteins involved in the secretory process, in addition to KATP channels in the plasma membrane (Eliasson et al., 1996; Hinke, 2009; Kang et al., 2011; Lehtihet et al., 2003; Renström et al., 2002; Shibasaki et al., 2014; Tian et al., 1998; Zhang et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Eliasson et al., 1996; Hinke, 2009; Kang et al., 2011; Lehtihet et al., 2003; Renström et al., 2002; Shibasaki et al., 2014; Tian et al., 1998; Zhang et al., 2009.

claim: An application of glibenclamide under depolarized condition (30 mM extracellular K+) can still promote additional insulin secretion without further changes in [Ca2+]in.
source: Moreover, while the plasma membrane of β cells is strongly depolarized by raising the concentration of extracellular K+ to 30 mM, an application of glibenclamide under this depolarized condition can still promote additional insulin secretion without further changes in [Ca2+]in (Geng et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Geng et al., 2007.

claim: SpTx1 is a 54-residue protein toxin isolated from the venom of Scolopendra polymorpha.
source: In particular, a 54-residue protein toxin isolated from the venom of Scolopendra polymorpha, dubbed SpTx1, is the most potent inhibitor with a Kd of 15 nM (Ramu et al., 2018; Ramu and Lu, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Ramu et al., 2018 and Ramu and Lu, 2019.

claim: SpTx1 is the most potent inhibitor of hKir6.2 with a Kd of 15 nM.
source: In particular, a 54-residue protein toxin isolated from the venom of Scolopendra polymorpha, dubbed SpTx1, is the most potent inhibitor with a Kd of 15 nM (Ramu et al., 2018; Ramu and Lu, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Ramu et al., 2018 and Ramu and Lu, 2019.

claim: The blood glucose level of overnight-fasted wild-type mice was 173 (±3.18) mg/dl in the following morning.
source: The blood glucose level of the overnight-fasted wild-type mice was 173 (±3.18) mg/dl in the following morning (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is a measurement reported in the study and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: A single intraperitoneal application of glibenclamide (40 mg/kg body weight) lowered the blood glucose level of wild-type mice by half at the end of a 2-hr observation period.
source: As expected, a single intraperitoneal application of glibenclamide (40 mg/kg body weight) lowered the blood glucose level of wild-type mice by half at the end of a 2-hr observation period whereas that of the vehicle dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO) did not have any meaningful effect.
evidence: This is an experimental result shown in Figure 1A.

claim: DMSO vehicle did not have any meaningful effect on blood glucose levels of wild-type mice.
source: As expected, a single intraperitoneal application of glibenclamide (40 mg/kg body weight) lowered the blood glucose level of wild-type mice by half at the end of a 2-hr observation period whereas that of the vehicle dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO) did not have any meaningful effect.
evidence: This is an experimental result shown in Figure 1A.

claim: SpTx1 at a dose of 1 mg/kg neither had discernible effect on the blood glucose levels of wild-type mice nor caused other noticeable differences during the observation period.
source: SpTx1 at a dose of 1 mg/kg neither had discernible effect on the blood glucose levels of wild-type mice (Figure 1B) nor caused other noticeable differences during the observation period, when compared to wild-type mice administered with the vehicle saline.
evidence: This is an experimental result shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Using total blood volume, the dose of 1 mg/kg SpTx1 is calculated to be 3 µM, ~200 times the Kd value of SpTx1 against hKir6.2.
source: Using total blood volume, this dose of SpTx1 is calculated to be 3 µM, ~200 times the Kd value of SpTx1 against hKir6.2.
evidence: This is a calculation based on the dose administered and known Kd value.

claim: SpTx1 failed to alter insulin secretion from wild-type mouse islets in the presence of either 7 or 15 mM glucose at concentrations between 0.2 and 1 μM.
source: In this concentration range, SpTx1 failed to alter insulin secretion in the presence of either 7 or 15 mM glucose (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is an experimental result shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Dissociated β cells exhibited altered electrophysiological properties, including a much greater cell-to-cell variation in glucose sensitivity, compared with the cells in isolated islets.
source: Previous studies reported that dissociated β cells exhibited altered electrophysiological properties, for example, a much greater cell-to-cell variation in glucose sensitivity, compared with the cells in isolated islets (Salomon and Meda, 1986; Scarl et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Salomon and Meda, 1986 and Scarl et al., 2019.

claim: In a typical mouse islet, up to 80% of the cells are β cells.
source: In a typical mouse islet, up to 80% of the cells are β cells (Steiner et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Steiner et al., 2010.

claim: In wild-type mouse islets, glucose and glibenclamide dramatically depolarize Vm but SpTx1, despite its high concentration (>10 times the Kd value for hKir6.2), has no such effect.
source: Thus, in wild-type mouse islets, glucose and glibenclamide dramatically depolarize Vm but SpTx1, despite its high concentration (>10 times the Kd value for hKir6.2), has no such effect.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: The amino acid sequences of hKir6.2 and mKir6.2 are 96% identical.
source: Indeed, the amino acid sequences of hKir6.2 and mKir6.2 are extremely similar but not identical (96% identity).
evidence: This is a comparison of known protein sequences.

claim: SpTx1 inhibits hKATP channels comprised of hKir6.2 and hSUR1 with an apparent Kd of 15 nM.
source: The concentration dependence of current inhibition by SpTx1 was fitted using a model for the toxin-to-channel interaction with one-to-one stoichiometry, yielding an apparent Kd of 15 and 673 nM for hKATP and mKATP, respectively (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is an experimental result shown in Figure 3E.

claim: SpTx1 inhibits mKATP channels comprised of mKir6.2 and mSUR1 with an apparent Kd of 673 nM.
source: The concentration dependence of current inhibition by SpTx1 was fitted using a model for the toxin-to-channel interaction with one-to-one stoichiometry, yielding an apparent Kd of 15 and 673 nM for hKATP and mKATP, respectively (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is an experimental result shown in Figure 3E.

claim: SpTx1 inhibits mKATP with a much lower potency than hKATP.
source: Clearly, SpTx1 inhibits mKATP with a much lower potency than hKATP.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the Kd values measured in the study.

claim: SpTx1 inhibited currents through hKir6.2 + hSUR1 and hKir6.2 + mSUR1 with high affinities.
source: SpTx1 inhibited currents through hKir6.2 + hSUR1 and hKir6.2 + mSUR1 with high affinities but, in contrast, the toxin inhibited currents through mKir6.2 + mSUR1 and mKir6.2 + hSUR1 with low affinities (Figure 3E, F).
evidence: This is an experimental result shown in Figure 3E, F.

claim: SpTx1 inhibited currents through mKir6.2 + mSUR1 and mKir6.2 + hSUR1 with low affinities.
source: SpTx1 inhibited currents through hKir6.2 + hSUR1 and hKir6.2 + mSUR1 with high affinities but, in contrast, the toxin inhibited currents through mKir6.2 + mSUR1 and mKir6.2 + hSUR1 with low affinities (Figure 3E, F).
evidence: This is an experimental result shown in Figure 3E, F.

claim: Differences in the two pore-forming orthologous Kir6.2 themselves, but not in their SUR1, primarily underlie the observed differential SpTx1 affinities.
source: The above two lines of results indicate that differences in the two pore-forming orthologous Kir6.2 themselves, but not in their SUR1, primarily underlie the observed differential SpTx1 affinities, and are consistent with the idea that SpTx1 inhibits currents through KATP channels by interacting with Kir6.2 (Ramu et al., 2018; Ramu and Lu, 2019).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from experimental data in Figures 3 and 4, supported by citations to Ramu et al., 2018 and Ramu and Lu, 2019.

claim: SpTx1 inhibits currents through KATP channels by interacting with Kir6.2.
source: The above two lines of results indicate that differences in the two pore-forming orthologous Kir6.2 themselves, but not in their SUR1, primarily underlie the observed differential SpTx1 affinities, and are consistent with the idea that SpTx1 inhibits currents through KATP channels by interacting with Kir6.2 (Ramu et al., 2018; Ramu and Lu, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Ramu et al., 2018 and Ramu and Lu, 2019, and by experimental data in the current study.

claim: The triple mutations (S103G, A107N, and E108V) in hKir6.2bgd lowered the affinity for SpTx1 to the level of mKir6.2bgd.
source: The triple mutations (S103G, A107N, and E108V), making this segment identical to that in mKir6.2, lowered the affinity of hKir6.2bgd for SpTx1 to the level of mKir6.2bgd (Figure 4A, black squares).
evidence: This is an experimental result shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The E108V mutation alone lowered the affinity of hKir6.2bgd to about that of mKir6.2bgd.
source: Indeed, the E108V mutation alone lowered the affinity of hKir6.2bgd to about that of mKir6.2bgd (Figure 4C, triangles versus orange curve) whereas the other two point mutations had little effects on the affinity of hKir6.2bgd (Figure 4C, squares and inverse triangles versus blue curve).
evidence: This is an experimental result shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The S103G and A107N point mutations had little effects on the affinity of hKir6.2bgd for SpTx1.
source: Indeed, the E108V mutation alone lowered the affinity of hKir6.2bgd to about that of mKir6.2bgd (Figure 4C, triangles versus orange curve) whereas the other two point mutations had little effects on the affinity of hKir6.2bgd (Figure 4C, squares and inverse triangles versus blue curve).
evidence: This is an experimental result shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The reversed triple or single-V108E mutation conferred high SpTx1 affinity on mKir6.2bgd comparable to the SpTx1 affinity of hKir6.2bgd.
source: Either the reversed triple or single-V108E mutation conferred such a high SpTx1 affinity on mKir6.2bgd that was comparable to the SpTx1 affinity of hKir6.2bgd (Figure 5A–C, F, triangles and circles versus blue curve).
evidence: This is an experimental result shown in Figure 5A–C, F.

claim: The mKir6.2-V108E mutation conferred the high SpTx1 affinity of hKATP channels on mKATP channels coexpressed with mSUR1.
source: Indeed, the mKir6.2V108E (mKir6.2-V108E) mutation conferred the high SpTx1 affinity of hKATP channels on mKATP channels coexpressed with mSUR1 (Figure 5D, G, inverse triangles versus cyan curve).
evidence: This is an experimental result shown in Figure 5D, G.

claim: The hKir6.2-E108V mutation conferred the low SpTx1 affinity of mKATP channels on hKATP channels coexpressed with hSUR1.
source: Conversely, the hKir6.2-E108V mutation conferred the low SpTx1 affinity of mKATP channels on hKATP channels coexpressed with hSUR1 (Figure 5E, G, squares versus vermilion curve).
evidence: This is an experimental result shown in Figure 5E, G.

claim: The low affinity of mKATP channels for SpTx1 reflects a residue variant, valine versus glutamate, at amino acid position 108 located in the extracellular vestibule of the pore.
source: The above results demonstrate that the low affinity of mKATP channels for SpTx1 reflects a residue variant, valine versus glutamate, at amino acid position 108 located in the extracellular vestibule of the pore.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the mutagenesis experiments shown in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: SpTx1 inhibits the KATP channel by blocking Kir6.2's ion-conduction pore.
source: This finding in turn strengthens the notion that SpTx1 inhibits the KATP channel by blocking Kir6.2's ion-conduction pore (Ramu et al., 2018; Ramu and Lu, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Ramu et al., 2018 and Ramu and Lu, 2019, and by experimental data in the current study.

claim: SpTx1 at 0.2 µM caused a small depolarization in EndomKir6.2V108E β cells in nominal glucose-free condition, insufficient to elicit action potentials.
source: In a nominal glucose-free condition, SpTx1 at 0.2 µM, 10 times higher than the Kd value for V108E-carrying mKir6.2 (+mSUR1), caused a small depolarization (Figure 6A, orange segment); this SpTx1-induced Vm depolarization was, however, insufficient to elicit action potentials in comparison to that induced by high glucose challenge or glibenclamide that elicited action potentials (Figure 6A, blue and pink segments).
evidence: This is an experimental result shown in Figure 6A.

claim: With 5 mM glucose, SpTx1 at 0.2 µM caused variable Vm depolarization in EndomKir6.2V108E β cells without eliciting any action potentials.
source: With 5 mM glucose, SpTx1 at 0.2 µM caused (variable) Vm depolarization without eliciting any action potentials, which was again less than that induced by high glucose challenge or glibenclamide (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is an experimental result shown in Figure 6B.

claim: With 8 mM glucose, SpTx1 at 0.2 µM strongly depolarized Vm and elicited action potentials in EndomKir6.2V108E β cells.
source: However, with 8 mM glucose, SpTx1 at 0.2 µM strongly depolarized Vm and elicited action potentials (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is an experimental result shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The impact of SpTx1 on Vm depends on the glucose concentration.
source: Thus, the impact of SpTx1 on Vm depends on the glucose concentration.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from experimental data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Inclusion of 0.5 μM SpTx1 in the perifusion solution potentiated insulin secretion from EndomKir6.2V108E islets in 10 mM glucose to a level between that in 10 mM glucose alone and in 10 mM glucose plus glibenclamide.
source: Inclusion of 0.5 μM SpTx1 in the perifusion solution potentiated insulin secretion in 10 mM glucose to a level between that in 10 mM glucose alone and in 10 mM glucose plus glibenclamide (Figure 7A, orange trace).
evidence: This is an experimental result shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Following removal of high glucose, which also washed out extracellularly bound SpTx1, insulin secretion from EndomKir6.2V108E islets returned to the baseline level.
source: Following removal of high glucose by subsequent perifusion with a solution containing 3 mM glucose, which also washed out extracellularly bound SpTx1, insulin secretion returned to the baseline level.
evidence: This is an experimental result shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Whether added earlier or at the same time as raising the glucose concentration, SpTx1 had comparable potentiating effects on GSIS from EndomKir6.2V108E islets in 10 mM glucose.
source: We found that, whether added earlier or at the same time as raising the glucose concentration, SpTx1 had comparable potentiating effects on GSIS in 10 mM glucose (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is an experimental result shown in Figure 7B.

claim: In the presence of nonstimulating 3 mM glucose, glibenclamide triggered sizable secretion of insulin from EndomKir6.2V108E islets.
source: In the presence of nonstimulating 3 mM glucose, glibenclamide triggered sizable secretion of insulin (Figure 7C, purple trace) whereas SpTx1 caused no detectable insulin secretion above the baseline level (Figure 7B, blue trace).
evidence: This is an experimental result shown in Figure 7C.

claim: In the presence of nonstimulating 3 mM glucose, SpTx1 caused no detectable insulin secretion above the baseline level from EndomKir6.2V108E islets.
source: In the presence of nonstimulating 3 mM glucose, glibenclamide triggered sizable secretion of insulin (Figure 7C, purple trace) whereas SpTx1 caused no detectable insulin secretion above the baseline level (Figure 7B, blue trace).
evidence: This is an experimental result shown in Figure 7B.

claim: In the presence of 3 mM glucose, 0.5 μM SpTx1 did not stimulate insulin secretion above the baseline level from EndomKir6.2V108E islets but did markedly potentiate insulin secretion in the presence of 16.7 mM glucose.
source: In the presence of 3 mM glucose, 0.5 μM SpTx1 did not stimulate insulin secretion above the baseline level but did markedly potentiate insulin secretion in the presence of 16.7 mM glucose (Figure 7D, blue trace versus black trace), albeit less than that potentiated by 1 μM glibenclamide (Figure 7D, blue trace versus purple trace).
evidence: This is an experimental result shown in Figure 7D.

claim: As the SpTx1 concentration was increased to 2 μM, SpTx1 potentiated insulin secretion from EndomKir6.2V108E islets in the presence of 16.7 mM glucose to a level comparable to that caused by 1 μM glibenclamide.
source: As we increased the SpTx1 concentration to 2 μM, SpTx1 potentiated insulin secretion in the presence of 16.7 mM glucose to a level comparable to that caused by 1 μM glibenclamide (Figure 7D, vermilion trace versus purple trace in the ~30 to ~60 min region).
evidence: This is an experimental result shown in Figure 7D.

claim: At equivalent concentrations, glibenclamide and SpTx1 did not have comparable abilities as primary insulin secretagogues; SpTx1 stimulated much less insulin secretion than glibenclamide did in nonstimulating 3 mM glucose.
source: However, at these equivalent concentrations, glibenclamide and SpTx1 did not have comparable abilities as primary insulin secretagogues; SpTx1 stimulated much less insulin secretion than glibenclamide did as evidenced by their differing effects in nonstimulating 3 mM glucose (Figure 7D, vermilion trace versus purple trace in the ~20 to ~30 min region).
evidence: This is an experimental result shown in Figure 7D.

claim: 100 µM diazoxide lowered the insulin secretion from EndomKir6.2V108E islets in 16.7 mM glucose to the baseline level.
source: Furthermore, 100 µM diazoxide lowered the insulin secretion in 16.7 mM glucose to the baseline level.
evidence: This is an experimental result shown in Figure 7E.

claim: SpTx1 at 1 µM, but not 0.02 µM, could effectively boost GSIS from EndomKir6.2V108E islets in the presence of diazoxide.
source: SpTx1 at 1 µM, but not 0.02 µM, could effectively boost GSIS in the presence of diazoxide.
evidence: This is an experimental result shown in Figure 7E.

claim: An IV injection of SpTx1 (1 mg/kg) or its vehicle saline had no meaningful effect on the elevated blood glucose levels of diabetic Rosa26mKir6.2NDM mice.
source: We found that an IV injection of SpTx1 (1 mg/kg) or its vehicle saline had no meaningful effect on the elevated blood glucose levels of diabetic Rosa26mKir6.2NDM mice and did not trigger a rise of insulin in the plasma of their circulating blood collected during the observation period (Figure 8A, C, filled and open orange triangles).
evidence: This is an experimental result shown in Figure 8A, C.

claim: SpTx1 (1 mg/kg) did not trigger a rise of insulin in the plasma of diabetic Rosa26mKir6.2NDM mice.
source: We found that an IV injection of SpTx1 (1 mg/kg) or its vehicle saline had no meaningful effect on the elevated blood glucose levels of diabetic Rosa26mKir6.2NDM mice and did not trigger a rise of insulin in the plasma of their circulating blood collected during the observation period (Figure 8A, C, filled and open orange triangles).
evidence: This is an experimental result shown in Figure 8A, C.

claim: A single bolus application of glibenclamide (40 mg/kg) or its vehicle DMSO neither markedly lowered the elevated blood glucose level nor caused a rise of insulin in the plasma of diabetic Rosa26mKir6.2NDM-V108E mice during the observation period.
source: A single bolus application of glibenclamide (40 mg/kg) or its vehicle DMSO neither markedly lowered the elevated blood glucose level nor caused a rise of insulin in the plasma (Figure 8A, C, filled and open blue circles) of diabetic Rosa26mKir6.2NDM-V108E mice during the observation period.
evidence: This is an experimental result shown in Figure 8A, C.

claim: The ineffectiveness of acute glibenclamide treatments in Rosa26mKir6.2NDM-V108E mice is consistent with the ineffectiveness of acute glibenclamide treatments reported in the original study of Rosa26mKir6.2NDM mice.
source: This finding is consistent with the ineffectiveness of acute glibenclamide treatments reported in the original study of Rosa26mKir6.2NDM mice (Remedi et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Remedi et al., 2009.
